I'm 33 years old, and I've been farming my family's land in Quzhou County since I finished middle school. Around here, we all follow the same pattern — winter wheat and summer maize on the same plot. That's what my father did, that's what my neighbors do, and that's what the land and weather here suit best. I've got about 8 mu of good flat land, so this year I'll stick with what works.

For the winter wheat, I'll sow about 8 mu in October after the autumn harvest. I'll use an improved variety — probably *Luyuan 502* or *Jimai 22*, the same kinds everyone in the village trusts. Before sowing, I'll do rotary tillage to break up the stubble and level the field. I'll put down compound fertilizer as basal dressing — around 22 kg of P₂O₅ and 8 kg of K₂O per mu, plus some nitrogen. Then I'll topdress with urea at jointing to bring total nitrogen up to about 65 kg per mu. Wheat is thirsty, so I'll irrigate four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, then at jointing, heading, and grain filling. I'll spray pesticides about four times total — herbicide once before tillering, insecticide twice for aphids and armyworm, and fungicide once to prevent rust. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 1,000 jin per mu, maybe a bit more.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I'll immediately plant summer maize — 8 mu again. For maize, I always buy hybrid seed from the shop; *Denghai 605* is what most of us use now because it yields well and resists lodging. I'll sow it no-tillage right into the wheat stubble to save time and keep moisture. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat — about 24 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. I'll irrigate twice, once at the seedling stage and once at the big flare stage, because two good waterings are usually enough if the summer rains come. I'll spray insecticide twice for corn borer and aphids, plus herbicide once. With this hybrid, I should get about 1,100 jin per mu.

This is the safest plan. The prices for wheat and maize are steady, the inputs are available at the village cooperative, and I know these crops. I don't want to gamble on cotton or vegetables — one bad price swing and I'd lose money.
